utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I saw you struggling to stand. I have been advised of your injury. You need not stand at any time. Today we are hearing the witness Wil Fagel. The procedural history in relation to this witness's evidence is known to the parties. I don't have to repeat it. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I propose to do is to ask you to lead the witness in chief, in chief, in relation to the document 1D25.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will do my best. Understanding that the nature of the opinion that's going to be elicited by Doctorandus Fagel has been reviewed by this Chamber. It's a handwriting comparison. Inherent in any type of comparison, a document is compared to other documents, so I think that this was very well-noted by the Chamber in terms of its inseparable nature of the discussion of 1D25 with the other documents. If I could be allowed to then lead or present evidence as I go through that comparison. I understand the Chamber's instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the examination-in-chief will be confined to 1D25, bearing in mind, of course, that you will not be allowed to lead any other evidence because that evidence, which the Chamber has already determined, doesn't qualify as rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could please ask the Chamber a clarification. Is the Chamber indicating that the Prosecution cannot lead evidence as to the comparison of 1D25 with any other documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can use whatever documents you provided, but you can't use the P exhibits. You wanted to say something, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I know where the Prosecution's going, this is the slippery slope, is they are going to use the signature comparisons from the omitted documents that were ruled as being not-admissible, so they're basically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it comes to light during the course of evidence that this needs to be revisited, could we please -- just because his nature of his evidence is that he is a handwriting expert, so he's comparing those signatures, but could we please see how the testimony unfolds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've already given the ruling on it. Let's proceed. Bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctorandus Fagel.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: My name is Wil Fagel. I'm a forensic handwriting examiner working for the Netherlands Forensic Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain what a forensic handwriting examiner is.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: A forensic handwriting examiner is an expert who --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... with known writings from, for example, suspects with the purpose to assess whether these handwritings or signatures have been produced by this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the Netherlands Forensic Institute?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Netherlands Forensic Institute is autonomous agency under the Dutch Ministry of Justice which performs several kinds of forensic examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How long have you been a forensic handwriting examiner?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Next month, it will be 26 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctorandus Fagel, during the course of your testimony here today, it will be important that you observe a pause after the questions that are being asked to you in order to allow the translators to translate for other members who are present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry for answering too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many handwriting comparisons have you conducted as a forensic handwriting examiner over the past 26 years?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I haven't counted them exactly, but it must be over 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you hold any certifications as a forensic handwriting examiner?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, I have a certified by the Netherlands Forensic Institute and recertified every four years to do kind of exams, every four years, and I'm a member of the GFS, which is a European association of forensic handwriting and document examiners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you been previously qualified as an expert before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders the curriculum vitae of this witness into evidence. It is ERN 0642-9654 through 0642-9655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, based on the qualifications of the witness the Prosecution tenders Doctorandus Fagel as an expert in forensic handwriting analysis. May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is a forensic comparative handwriting examination?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: A forensic comparative handwriting examination is an examination where questions, handwriting and/or questions, signatures are analysed and compared with known samples of writing or signatures from another person, some person, maybe a suspect or a witness, to assess whether the questions, handwritings, or signatures have been written by this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are the phases of a forensic comparative handwriting examination?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: There are four phases. The first phase is the analysis of the features of the questions and the comparison samples; the second phase is a comparison of these features; The third phase is the interpretation, weighing of the similarities and differences of these comparison; and finally, last phase is the -- drawing a conclusion from these findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are the main categories of handwriting characteristics?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: There are three main categories. The first main category are general features, general handwriting characteristics; the second category are layout characteristics; and the third general category are micro-characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are general characteristics?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: General characteristics are features that concern the general appearance of the handwriting, like overall slant of the writing, the size of the writing, the overall line quality, the overall pen pressure, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are layout characteristics?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Layout characteristics with handwritten text, for example, letters may refer to, for example, the word distances, width of left and right margins, distances between lines of writing, and when it's about signatures, it may, for example, refer to placement of the signature within a preprinted box.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are micro- characteristics?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Micro-characteristics refer to the proportions, the size -- no, sorry, the form, the shape, I mean, and the proportions of the individual elements within the handwriting. When it's text, it may be letters or numbers, et cetera. In signatures, it might be also other patterns than the standard patterns which are in written text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What differences are there in a comparative handwriting examination of a signature as opposed to handwritten text?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: In general, when comparing signature we look at -- signatures we look at the same features as when we look at -- when we compare handwritten text, only in -- when comparing signatures, some features are more important, like line quality, pen pressure, because signatures are more often subject of a simulation than handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is a bona fide signature as compared to a mala fide signature?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: A bona fide signature is a signature which have been written by the signatory and maybe normal general signature, but also an alternative signature which he might use for special purposes. And a mala fide signature is, for example, simulated signature, copied signature by someone else than the signatory, or it may also be a so-called autoforgery where someone makes his own signature in such a way that it looks like a simulation so to be later able to deny that he wrote the signature. Alternatively, people may -- when forging someone's signature, if they don't know what it exactly looks like, they might just fantasise the signature, a so-called fictitious signature. Also, the owner of the signatory signature may also write another signature than he usually does so as to later to deny that he wrote the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the forensic comparative handwriting examination method you described accredited by any institutions?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Our method and procedures are accredited by the Dutch Council For Accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you attach a document describing this accredited methodology to your report as an appendix?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this the method of comparative handwriting examination that you used in this case in relation to your 8th of October, 2008, report?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders the witness's 8th October, 2008, report into evidence along with its appendices. It is ERN 0642-8808 through 0642-8820.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would object based on the ruling of the Court that the report contains analysis of which the evidence the underlying analysis is based on has been ruled inadmissible by the Court. Therefore, the report that incorporates that inadmissible evidence should also be inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We won't allow the report in evidence. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Still please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I lead at this time? May I lead the witness at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May you lead --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean ask him leading questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it relates to issues that are not contentious, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctorandus Fagel, you received materials to conduct a forensic handwriting comparison on the 15th of September, 2008; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The materials that you received for examination included five documents with questioned signatures and nine documents with known signatures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the five documents with questioned signatures, you performed a forensic mutual handwriting comparison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The five questioned in reference, one, lack of foundation; two, that would be my understanding that these would be the inadmissible matters that we've already been ruled on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he conducted a handwriting comparison. He has to compare 1D25 to some other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but we have already ruled that we are not allowing it. You must respect the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctorandus Fagel, it is possible to conduct a mutual handwriting comparison of one document unless you can compare it to other documents?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I understand your question, but I can only compare two or more signatures. I cannot compare one signature with itself, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So if you have a signature on a document, the specific document that you were given with respect to this matter that ends in ERN 568 - which for the record is 1D25 - are you unable to offer an opinion here before the Tribunal unless you are able to reference the other signatures on the other documents that you compared it to?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I cannot give an opinion on just one signature if I cannot compare it to anything else, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to this case, you did review multiple signatures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you were able to formulate opinions to a reasonable degree of certainty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, refers to an analysis that would incorporate inadmissible evidence. May I voir dire the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: May I voir dire the witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: From a foundational perspective, I believe that the witness can offer an opinion using known signatures and a single signature. I think if the Prosecution asked him that question, he might get a different answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is -- Mr. Alarid will have plenty of opportunity to cross-examine this witness. At this time, the Prosecution is eliciting evidence about the very nature of what Doctorandus Fagel did in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain what a mutual handwriting comparison is?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: What we -- when we compare a questioned signature, let me state first it is possible to compare one questioned signature with a number of known or reference samples to give an opinion whether or not this single questioned signature was or was not written by the same person. But if we have more questioned signatures, we first perform a mutual comparison of these questioned signatures to see whether the assumption that these have all been written by the same person is justified. If they are very consistent, then we take them as one group of signatures to compare with the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is that what you did in this case?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please explain the observations that you made --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I haven't even asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think it's obvious that you're going to mutual examination if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the question first. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctorandus Fagel, did you group four signatures together for mutual comparison against known signatures in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Don't answer the question. I'd like to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The position is as follows: Mr. Weber explained that the Prosecution gave Mr. Fagel nine documents. He can compare 1D25 with the five documents that are not the four Prosecution documents that have been ruled inadmissible. So you can proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you provided with a document that contained an unknown signature ending in ERN 568?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What did you do with that document?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I compared it with the other questioned signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After you compared it to the other questioned signatures, what did you do with those signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I noticed that -- that they have a very similar general design, and I noticed that they were in such a way similar that they looked to me almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe that this is exactly what we're getting into again. He is referring to the mutual analysis, not the supposed known samples that were provided by the Prosecution. These are exactly what the Court's ruled on that he has just testified to. Move to strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wish you wouldn't say move to strike. We don't have that procedure here, Mr. Alarid. The question that you asked, Mr. Weber, does it relate to the five documents that are not the four Prosecution documents which we have ruled inadmissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, because of the identical nature of all four of the signatures, he took -- he made a transparency and compared that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You cannot ask him for the comparison with the documents that we have ruled inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But it's upon that transparency that he created --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, the attorney is testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can't do that, and you must respect the Court's ruling. If you are not prepared to respect it, then there are other measures to adopt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. It was that transparency that he then compared to the known signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't re-argue the point. Just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the specific document that ends in ERN 568, did you make any observations with respect to the stamp on that document?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I only got a copy of this document, so I couldn't observe whether the stamp was made first before the document was signed or after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you got only a photocopy of that document. Can the possibility of tampering be excluded if only photocopies are available for analysis?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No, it clearly cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to conduct a comparison between the questioned signature for which ERN 568 was a part of with the known signatures provided to you?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you conduct this comparison?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I first look at the general -- at the design of the signature, whether it was similar or not, and though there are - let me see - they have some similarity in overall design. There are also a number of differences between this questioned signature and the referenced known signature of Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple questions about the known signatures before we discuss those differences. With respect to the nine known documents with the signature of Risto Perisic, were there original signatures available for your analysis of the known signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, lack of foundation. No evidence has been led as to how these are known signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lead that evidence, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctorandus Fagel, you were provided with documents which you took to be known signatures of Risto Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we usually call reference signatures. It's just a terminology. We call them known signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And among these documents, you had original signatures for comparison.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: There were two original signatures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on the availability of originals, were you able to -- well, were there any indications that show any signs of tampering with the known signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No, in the -- there were no signs of tampering in the known signatures or reference signatures, if you want, as far as I could tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did the reference signatures show a sufficient degree of complexity for analysis?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the lower portion of ERN 0642-8811 on the screen. This is page 4 of the witness's report, which begins at ERN 0642-8808.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. The report's been held inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just showing -- there's a figure in it that he did a comparison. I'm eliciting testimony relating to that figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please have page 4 of the lower portion of this document. Specifically, could we please zoom in on the figure that's depicted at the lower portion of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You are now being shown the lower portion, figure 1, on your 8th October, 2008, report. What does this figure depict?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: In top you can see a questioned signature, and the lower two signatures are two of the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the characteristics that you observed that were different between the questioned signature and the known signatures in this figure?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: If you look at the questioned signature, you can see it has a big loop in the top of the first element which is absent in the reference signatures. Furthermore, the questioned signature has a P-shaped element at about one-third of the length of the signature, and the downstroke of this element retraces the upstroke. In the known signatures, there's a clear space between the downstroke and the upstroke. Furthermore, the oval part of the P shape in the questioned signature is practically absent in the known signatures. Then there are a number of wave-like movements in the middle of the questioned signature. These differ in shape from those in the known signatures. In the questioned signature, they are more like arc gates, whereas in the known signatures they are more like garland-form shapes. Then there's a long stretch, a cross-bar type of line in the top at the end of the questioned signature which is absent in the known signatures. And finally, the questioned signature has a down stroke at the end, whereas the known signatures ends with a more upward movement. So these are the most apparent differences between the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time would tender a saved copy of this figure into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What were your findings with respect to the comparison of the questioned signature and the known signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: My findings were that -- my findings did not support the proposition that the signature -- that the questioned signature was originally written by Risto Perisic or by the producer of the reference signatures by that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you come to conclusion as to whether or not the questioned signatures were a bona fide or mala fide signature? Without stating that opinion at this time, did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Whether the questioned signatures were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whether the questioned signatures were bona fide or mala fide?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, to the use questioned signatures. That would be referring to inadmissible evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution plans on respecting the Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you able to form an opinion as to whether or not the questioned signatures were bona fide or mala fide? Just a simple yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you able to provide that opinion unless you are able to discuss the other unquestioned signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it Dr. Fagel?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: It's pronounced like Fahel, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Fahel is fine. I can pronounce that. Thank you. Now, let's talk a little bit about what you used as the comparison signatures and otherwise believed to be bona fide. Can we do that first?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who provided the supposed bona fide signatures to you?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: It was provided by the -- do I have to name the person?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, no. Just the agency would be fine.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: The ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in being provided those signatures, were you aware that the Defence of Milan Lukic had been attempting to subpoena Risto Perisic to come to The Hague to identify documents?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No, I had no information whatsoever about this case. I didn't even know the name of the accused by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And in referring to the supposed bona fide signatures, were you given any background or foundational information as to when the signatures were written, in what context, how?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No, only, of course, there are some dates mentioned with the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: So that's known information. Otherwise, I had no information on how they were produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, obviously, in a best-case scenario, you would want to have the actual author of the alleged signatures present to give numerous samples; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, but it's -- if the questioned signatures have been produced several years ago, then when you ask someone to -- several years later to produce a number of signatures, especially for the investigation, he might change his signature, or there might have been changes in the signature during these years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, yeah, because I was digging through some old paperwork, and I dug out a driver's licence I had signed right out of high school, and my signature has totally changed between my adult signature and high school. Is that uncommon for signatures to change over time?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Maybe between your -- when someone is younger. When he is still in high school and later, there may be strong differences, but during a normal adult lifetime, normally signatures don't change too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. But there can be fluctuations over time; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: There can be some fluctuations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And some of those fluctuations can also be -- because of the physical abilities of the person changed. They can be signing that day with an injury or not feeling well. There can be other things that can affect the signature on a particular day; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to the supposed bona fide signature, like I said, it would be best for you to have the person here to sign a few times to even compare against what otherwise is considered bona fide; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No. We prefer to have signatures which have been produced about the same time as the questioned signature, so-called contemporary signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And but for the information provided by the Office of the Prosecutor, did you do any independent research to establish when those purported bona fide signatures had been produced?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No, nothing. Only, of course, the dates which were mentioned with the signatures, I assumed these were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, do you read Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No. I can read a little bit, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, even though the names above the purported signatures are in the Latin alphabet, would it surprise you that the signature is in the Cyrillic alphabet?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No, I know it's like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution asked you sort of a leading question in the sense that: "Did you see any sign of tampering of the known or reference signatures?" What tampering would you expect to find in the known signatures in response to the OTP's question?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: If signatures are written -- not written fluently but, rather, hesitating with a lot of pen lifts, for example, and -- no, not reiterated - sorry, I don't know the words - then this might indicate a forgery, but I didn't see any of these indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What if them are all forgeries? All the ones that are meant as a reference, what if they're all forgeries by the same author?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Then we have a wrong comparison material. But when I get a number of reference signatures, I assume that they are true reference signatures from the person, alleged person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, obviously, if the alleged person were here and identified those, well, that would be added evidence to bolster your opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: If they would admit that these signatures were his?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to kind of lay a little bit of a foundation, my grandfather was a local politician for many years, and he had had a stamp of which to sign cheques for the grocery store and also to sign his official documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, the relevance of this about Mr. Alarid's grandfather to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, it was to lay a little foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you know Mr. Alarid is anecdotal --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- if nothing else, so we will allow him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, how does a possibility of a stamp play into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Well, in the first place, what we examine is whether the signatures were written by a person, not whether they were stamped by the same person. And even if a stamp was used, you might find some differences in inking when you make several stamps, and I didn't find any difference between the signatures I examined in the density of the ink.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask you about a stamp, is a stamp, when we create one for the printmaker or the stampmaker, you sign your signature, and then the printmaker makes a block of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So a stamp is sort of like a driver's licence picture. It's sort of as good as the time you made it, and you're stuck with it; is that fair, to use the anecdote?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, meaning if I write my signature -- I know I need to prepare a stamp some day, and I write my signature for the printmaker, that is the print block that goes. I may have to sort of live with it from that day forward.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Well, to change it, I got to get a new stamp made.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, if you want to use a stamp to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just if I don't like my driver's licence, I got to go back and get a new picture.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And so you don't have any idea if the questioned signature was part of a stamp?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it possible that persons in political roles or administrative roles use stamps in order to effectuate some of their daily business?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That would be possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the use of the stamp is also a good way for a small-town politician or maybe a police chief in charge of the Visegrad to avoid responsibility or have plausible deniability later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He testified to that, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How can he testify to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does he know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, maybe what reasons do people want their handwriting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'll tie it into something relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You talked about autoforgery. What's an autoforgery again?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: When someone on purpose changes his own handwriting. Sometimes they will, say, disguise his own signature so as to later deny that he wrote the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Now, might someone in questionable practices, i.e., maybe possibly committing war crimes, might want to use an autoforgery for certain things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How can he testify to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He is a handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. You're right, Your Honour. Maybe I'm going too far afield in terms of -- that's for argument in submissions more than it is for this witness to speculate on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So the fact of the matter is, though, is you can't exclude the use of a stamp for Risto Perisic for the questioned signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I cannot exclude it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And other than being told that the signatures that were the reference signatures are actual bona fide, you've done no research to actually verify that.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I have to read this question. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid just asked you a number of questions about the bona fide signatures. Were you able to determine whether or not the signature which is on document 5 -- ending in ERN 568 was a bona fide or mala fide signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation; no foundation was laid as to how he knew the bona fide signatures were as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He can answer the question. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could determine not on its own -- when I assessed the signature on its own, I cannot give an answer, but when I relate it to my observations in respect to the other signatures, I could determine this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the signature that's on document ending in ERN 568 a mala fide signature?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the basis of that opinion?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That there is -- the signature exactly matches the other three signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is where I'd say to strike, so I don't know what you'd prefer me to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you can't go into that. We have been through that already, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender the report of Doctorandus Fagel in evidence and ask the Chamber to consider it just for the limited purpose as it relates to document 1D25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we would object, Your Honour, so much as that's not how he conducted his analysis; therefore, there's no way to properly extricate that argument from his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We won't admit the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a number of questions about the known signatures that were provided to you. Is it correct there were nine of these?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Actually, two of the copied documents were copies of the two documents which I had an original, so there were totally seven reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were provided with nine documents --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- but you used only seven for the purposes of your comparison.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And the documents that were copies, was that 0024-7267 and 0024-7268 --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- were copies of 0064-1896 and 0064-1897?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And were the other documents that you used for comparison with the ERNs 0297-1870 --

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- and document 0324-6754 through 0324-6757?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, that last document that I read out, which was 0324-6754 through -57, is in evidence as Exhibit P317. The Prosecution would tender into evidence the explanation of the methodology that's attached to the expert's report, which is at 0642-8816 through 0642-8820.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Mr. Weber, does this methodology incorporate the mutual comparison?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid is in possession of this ERN. It does not include that. This is the explanation of his methodology. Instead of leading substantial evidence today regarding additional methodology, I believe it's most efficient to just tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P348, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender the individual page, which is appendix 2 to the witness's report, which is 0642-8815. This is the page that shows the known signatures only that were used in the witness's comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would also tender the seven -- actually, the nine documents used for his comparison, not for the truth of what the documents purportedly say, but as it relates to the witness's expert opinion here today, with the exception being P317, which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P350, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the known signatures that were provided to you, were you able to determine whether or not there was a normal variance in these signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And with respect to any time an individual signs a document, is there some degree of variation in how they sign the document?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: Yes, this is so-called natural variation. Every time you sign a signature, there are always differences between two signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the seven signatures that were known signatures, is there any indication that these documents are not from the same person?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No. They are very consistent, and the assumption that they have been written by the same person is supported by the fact that they are fluently written, show natural variation, and are very consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And there are no signs of autoforgery or anything of the like in those signatures?

utterances.speaker: WILHELMUES FAGEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Dr. Fagel, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I understand that you indicated that you would have your comments -- I believe we should be in private session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe we had indicated that closing arguments would be one hour each.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Subject to our pending motion, Your Honour, we asked for three hours in the motion to enlarge as well as asking for Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We won't allow three hours, Mr. Alarid. We won't allow three hours, Mr. Alarid. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Prosecution Closing Statement:

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, last July the trial of Sredoje and Milan Lukic began. Last week, the Prosecution filed its final trial brief summarising the evidence that is now before the Chamber and setting out its case of how that evidence establishes beyond a reasonable doubt the guilt of both accused. The brief details evidence of the killing of the men along the Drina River at Sase and at the Varda factory; it sets out the burning to death of over a hundred civilians in the houses on Pionirska Street and in Bikavac; the killing of Hajra Koric; and the mistreatment of civilian detainees at Uzamnica camp. By now, you will read this brief, and I will not attempt to summarise the Prosecution's's case in the limited time I have today. I will use my hour to address some of the points made in the final briefs of Sredoje and Milan Lukic. The Prosecution's case has gathered all the available witnesses and documents relevant to this indictment. Taken together and viewed as a unitary corpus of evidence, it establishes without doubt the guilt of both accused. Witnesses, now scattered across Europe, most having never spoken with each other since they each precariously escaped Visegrad, were brought to The Hague one by one to testify before you. They recounted their harrowing ordeals, describing the crimes of both accused. They corroborate each other and are in turn corroborated by the available physical and documentary evidence. They are reliable and credible witnesses. Their evidence also compellingly establishes the intent of the two accused to commit these crimes, their intent most evident in the Pionirska and Bikavac fires. In spite of the preparations made by Sredoje and Milan Lukic for the Pionirska fire and in spite of all efforts to kill those desperately trying to escape, eight people did survive the Pionirska fire. The six who are still living testified in person. Having fallen short of destroying every member of the Kurspahic family as Milan Lukic had asserted to Court Witness number 1, he and Sredoje Lukic would learn from their mistakes and take extra steps to secure the house in Bikavac before setting another group of Muslims ablaze two weeks later, both of them barricading the front entrance with a steel garage door. The Bikavac fire was carried out with the precision and the effectiveness that comes with premeditation. They nearly succeeded in killing all inside. Zehra Turjacanin, the sole survivor, escaped that inferno, driven by a desire to save her brother, her neighbours, and her friends from a similar fate. This is my only opportunity to make submissions regarding the final trial briefs of both accused, and while I trust the Chamber will carefully analyse all arguments and adopt only those that pass careful scrutiny, I do want to respond to some of the points that are raised in those briefs. Both Defence counsel raise as a central reason why you should acquit both accused is the inconsistencies that they have identified in the final trial briefs. They suggest to you that such inconsistencies indicate you cannot rely on the evidence of these witnesses. Your Honours are experienced jurists and have sufficient time on the bench to know that several witnesses viewing an event from different perspectives will invariably have differences between their accounts. Even witnesses who recount their evidence on several occasions can be expected to have minor differences between these retellings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but we have a problem with translation in B/C/S, namely the translator/interpreter are late for two paragraphs in transcript, so I kindly ask my learned friend so speak a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you would have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I haven't heard anything from the -- I'm wearing the headset so I can be mindful to the interpreters. If there is a problem, I certainly would ask them to advise me to slow down. I will continue at I think what is a slow pace, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed at a slightly slower pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The inconsistencies which Defence place great significance are simply a function of human memory and a function of different people seeing something from different perspectives. As VG-013 said at page 1089 of the transcript: "All of us who were there in that group, nobody can say exactly the same thing because they haven't seen all of them, the same things. One saw one part. Another saw another part." This astute comment is precisely the point that the Chamber must keep in mind when reviewing the evidence, and it is exactly what the Chamber has in this body of evidence, the independent accounts of all of the relevant witnesses. The large group of Kurspahics involved in the Pionirska fire were spread out over a significant area. The column was broken and disconnected as it made its way from the square in Visegrad to the Memic house on Pionirska Street. The Memic house had about 70 people spread out into several rooms on two floors. Some victims were already inside the Omeragic house while others were still trying to wake their children in the Memic house. Yet the Defence would have you view all of the events of this day as if the witnesses were sitting a theatre watching the same performance and suggest that any difference in recollection is evidence of dishonesty. The witnesses have recalled honestly what they saw. I submit that any inconsistencies are an indication of their honesty. Compared with the evidence of some of the Defence witnesses, identical recollections of insignificant events 16 years ago, it is that kind of consistency which is the hallmark of fabrication of witnesses who have discussed their testimony among themselves prior to coming into this Chamber. The Defence's own expert Dr. Hough explained very clearly that inconsistencies are expected and of themselves mean little. He expressed his view that three of the Prosecution witnesses were traumatised and that he would not be surprised that the trauma would manifest itself in their testimony. He said that with trauma victims, it is often "very difficult emotionally to recall and report on trauma experiences." It is stressful experience to pull up those memories. Dr. Hough said: "The degree to which that stress is heightened by anxiety ... the recall process can be subject to some distortion." Events can be reported in slightly different order and time sequences. He never suggested that these recollections were inherently unreliable or that inconsistencies are an indicator of unreliablity. He also said what many of us already know to be true, that due to the number of years that have passed, it would be unrealistic to expect perfect consistency. Even measured by the yard-stick of a Defence expert, the Prosecution witnesses' accounts have the ring of truth and together form a compelling body of evidence. I would now like to address the issue of identification. As Judge Robinson observed early in this case, the essential issue in the case is identification. The Prosecution final trial brief sets out in detail each of the witnesses, the survivors who knew one or both of the accused prior to the day they perpetrated these crimes. Defence witnesses from Visegrad as well as Prosecution witnesses are uniform in their assessment that the size and custom of Visegrad was such that people knew each other, if not always by name, very often by sight. Prosecution witnesses described in detail their basis for knowing the accused and recognising them at the scene of the crime. Some confirmed their recognition of the accused in court as well. Both Defence briefs erroneously link the ability of a witness to describe a perpetrator with their ability to recognise a perpetrator, suggesting that inconsistent descriptions indicate an unreliable recognition. As the Prosecution brief points out, there is an important difference between our ability as humans to recognise someone and our ability to describe someone. They are two different skills, and while most people are easily able to reliably recognise people they know, describing them is often something they do poorly. Children, infants, long before they can describe what their mother or father looks like, they are able to recognise them. Recognition is an essential instinctual skill that enables us to quickly identify those who present a danger and those who provide safety. If there is any doubt in your mind as to the difference between these two skills, consider this simple exercise. Have each one of you and your staff write down on a piece of paper my height, my weight, my hair colour, age, eye colour without prior discussion. If you do, I'm confident that no two will be the same, even if I were to stand here while you wrote your descriptions, and in fact there might be broad discrepancies between the descriptions, despite having seen me for a period of nearly a year under the bright lights of this courtroom. Yet every day when I appear before you, you instantly recognise me, and if we encounter each other years from now, you will again recognise me. You will have no difficulty recognising me, but you may have difficulty correctly describing me. There were approximately 35 police officers in Visegrad prior to the conflict. Why is it unreasonable, as the Defence of Sredoje Lukic suggests, for witnesses to have known Sredoje Lukic, either by sight or by name? Consider our own everyday experience here. There are over 150 different people working in the security department of this Tribunal. While we may come to know some by name, most we do not, yet we recognise our security staff when we encounter them each day here, in this courtroom, at the check-points downstairs. We recognise them when we meet them in the store on Saturday or see them on the queue waiting for a movie. Our innate ability as humans to recognise others we know is an accurate and reliable skill and one the Chamber can confidently rely upon. The witnesses in this case were continually encountering Sredoje Lukic over the course of their lives, much longer than our relatively short time here at the Tribunal. VG-38 knew Sredoje Lukic well, despite not knowing his name, and the fact that he first learned his name the night of the fire does nothing to detract from the reliability of his recognition. The Defence have raised a number of issues related to the credibility of individual witnesses. I want to address some of them here briefly. The first witness is MLD-025. A witness who testified with respect to the Drina River. For this, I would ask that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I apologise for the delay. I had to spend more time that I had anticipated dealing with a particular matter. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before the break I was beginning to talk about some of the specific issues raised with respect to the particular witnesses. I'd like to continue that with the discussion now of VG-115. Both accused vehemently challenge the evidence of VG-115, and challenged they must because she provides very damaging evidence regarding both accused. VG-115 is a Serb woman, the only Serb civilian from Visegrad who had the courage to come forward to describe what happened to her Muslim neighbours who were ethnically cleansed from the town, a woman who has no motive against either accused. She testified she hardly knew Milan Lukic, and she testified for the affection she had for Sredoje Lukic prior to the outbreak of the conflicts. The Defence despite their best efforts have been unable to establish with any evidence that she has a motive for falsely accusing either accused. In fact, the evidence of her motives are contained on pages 722 to 23 of the transcript where she said: "I have come here to prove the truth, and that truth is a small thing, namely what was it that those people ..." referring to the Avengers "... did in the city of Visegrad. I'm not actually defending the Muslim people or the Serbian people for that matter. I'm just here to tell what I've seen and what I've experienced." And in that attempt to discredit her, the Defence went out and took photographs from the veranda of the Smajic house where she was during the Pionirska fire. They absolutely confirm VG-115 and demonstrate her credibility when she described what she could see from her balcony. She said she saw smoke and flame. She never claimed to see the house itself. The photographs in evidence make clear that it is exactly what she would have seen, the smoke and fire rising from the inferno in the Omeragic house. The Prosecution submits that with everything that the Chamber now knows about this group, it is clear that VG-115's evidence is truthful, accurate, and corroborated in substantial part. The Defence's suggestion that her evidence should be summarily dismissed based upon the insufficiently reasoned opinion of the Vasiljevic Chamber is not warranted by the evidence before this Chamber. This Chamber has a far greater body of evidence and is in a far better position to evaluate the credibility of VG-115 and the other Prosecution witnesses than the Vasiljevic Chamber. The Sredoje Lukic Defence takes issue with her description of a sock on top of Sredoje Lukic's head on the afternoon of the Pionirska fire. While she did recall him covering his face with this sock during the Bikavac fire, she says something different with respect to the Pionirska fire. She simply says he was wearing it on his head, covering his shaved head. You will recall his head had been shaved while he was in captivity. A close examination of VG-115's testimony with regard to the sock is fully consistent with this view. Most telling, at the very point where VG-115 was attempting to explain this during her testimony, which is the portion relied on by the Sredoje Lukic Defence in their brief at paragraph 155, VG-115 was interrupted repeatedly by Defence counsel. Paragraph 155 states: "VG-115 was unable to provide any reasonable and satisfactory explanation..." for how she could identify Sredoje Lukic while wearing a stocking on his head. In fact, VG-115 was prevented from explaining. She was interrupted three times on page 781 alone preventing her from fully describing the way Sredoje Lukic wore this sock on his head. In fact, the manner in which VG-115 continues to mention the sock in the remainder of her testimony demonstrates that she is describing him wearing the sock on his head covering his hair, not as a full head sock over his whole head and face, as suggested by the Defence. When asked to identify the accused at the end of her testimony, she says, referring to the two accused: "Mr. Milan Lukic, wearing a black suit; next to him, Mr. Sredoje Lukic, who used to be bald and wear a sock over his head but now he has plenty of hair." The Sredoje Lukic Defence attempt to discredit VG-013's evidence by claiming that she did not see him during the Pionirska fire, and that Edhem Kurspahic did not know Sredoje Lukic, so she could not have heard Edhem identify Sredoje as he escorted people into the Omeragic house. With respect to the Edhem Kurspahic, the Defence contrast the evidence of VG-013 with VG-018's cursory remark that Edhem did not know Sredoje Lukic. Edhem was of the same generation as Hasib Kurspahic and was a life-long resident of the small village of Koritnik. There is no dispute that Sredoje Lukic was a frequent visitor to Koritnik, both while on patrol and to visit his good friend Huso Kurspahic. Edhem would have had the same opportunity to see Sredoje Lukic when he came to the small village. VG-018's response to the Defence counsel that Edhem Kurspahic and Sredoje Lukic did not know each other was a cursory conclusion. It was not based on Edhem telling her. It was an assumption on her part. The weight of the evidence before the Chamber strongly suggests that in this patriarchal society, the men of this village knew each other and would have known Sredoje Lukic, a prominent member of the community who regularly visited and patrolled the village. The claim that VG-013 did not see Sredoje Lukic is without merit. At paragraph 40 of the Defence brief, they claim that VG-013 "clearly testified that she did not see Sredoje Lukic on the 14th of June, 1992." In the full context of her evidence, it is clear that she physically saw him during the day, and that when the Lukic group returned at night and hurriedly moved the Kurspahic family in the Omeragic house, VG-013 did not see him but was told by Edhem Kurspahic that Sredoje Lukic was behind them. The Defence highlights that VG-013 apparently does not mention Sredoje Lukic in a video statement or a video interview admitted in this trial. It must be noted that this was an interview that was edited and is not a full account of what VG-013 said. In fact, the focus of the interview seemed to be something other than the crime at Pionirska Street. Please read the questioning about the video at transcript page 1130. Mr. Cepic places a transcript in front of VG-013 to see if she can authenticate it. It becomes clear that she is unable to read it. He then puts a single sentence from the transcript to her, a sentence limited to her saying that she was from Koritnik, that she had two sons, a daughter, and a husband, and they left Koritnik because people are dead. Nothing about the fire. She agrees, the tape is tendered, and he never puts to her as required under 90(h) his proposition that she did not mention Sredoje Lukic. Read the trial transcript. While the tape is being tendered, VG-013 is trying to ask questions about the tape; when was it made, where is it from? This is not evidence that she did not see Sredoje Lukic at Pionirska Street. The Defence also failed to note that long before this tape, VG-013 identified Sredoje Lukic as one of the perpetrators in a written statement from 1995 now in evidence as 1D29. We also know that she identified Sredoje Lukic as one of the perpetrators to Huso Kurspahic shortly after the fire. The Sredoje Lukic final trial brief places emphasis on what it characterises as striking evidence of VG-089 and is comprehensive and detailed description of Milan Lukic and the three men who were with him on the 14th of June, which corroborates the evidence of VG-101. The Sredoje Lukic Defence suggests that VG-089 is credible and that his observations of Milan Lukic and the other men with him on the day of the fire are reliable and credible. The Prosecution agrees with the Sredoje Lukic's position on this point. VG-089's observations of Milan Lukic in Visegrad on the day of the fire are indeed reliable. The Prosecution also agrees with the Sredoje Lukic Defence that the evidence of VG-101 and VG-089, two people who never met, corroborate each other. Where we disagree and where the Defence argument fails is in its assertion that if Sredoje Lukic was not in the car with VG-089 at the new bridge in town, he couldn't have later been at Pionirska Street. The argument makes the erroneous assumption that all of the perpetrators of the Pionirska fire were in the car with VG-089 and the two other boys who were killed, and we all know that this is simply not the case. VG-078 recalled approximately ten men all together being involved in the fire that night. Hasib Kurspahic and VG-115 provide the names of some of these other individuals. When VG-101 stated that she could only see four people, she was referring to a specific four people that she could see at a specific point in time, when she was being brought from the Memic house to the Omeragic house. There is no reasonable view of the evidence suggesting that there were only four members of the Lukic group present that night. In their final brief, Sredoje Lukic Defence make much of VG-038's response to a single confusing question and ask the Chamber to draw an unjustified inference from his answer. The question and answer are as follows: "Q. What do you know about my client, Sredoje Lukic, is only from that night, not from before? "A. Right." Is completely unclear from the context of the question what the words "what you know about my client" were intended to refer to. The Defence suggests that this is evidence that VG-038 did not know Sredoje Lukic before the Pionirska fire. The evidence makes clear that VG-038 did know Sredoje Lukic by sight, as a police officer. He learned his name the day of the Pionirska fire. The Sredoje Lukic Defence ends its discussion of VG-038's evidence with a misstatement of the evidence. At paragraph 81 of their brief, they claim that VG-038 testified he could not recognise the men who came in the evening because it was dark and because he did not dare to look at them. He said no such thing. In fact, in response to the question that is now in Prosecution Exhibit P044, Vasiljevic transcript at page 1377, he said: "Q. Were you able to see who it was who returned at this time?" VG-038 answered: "Yes. The same four men who searched us." VG-024, the Sredoje Lukic Defence urges the Chamber to disregard VG-024's evidence regarding seeing Sredoje Lukic at the end of June in Visegrad because she was not -- because that assertion was not contained previously in her statement. VG-024 gave a reasonable explanation for this at page 3216 of the transcript. When asked why she never mentioned it, she answered: "No one ever asked me about it. Yesterday when I was told that it was claimed that he was not in Visegrad at the time, I was a bit disappointed because I know that -- personally that he and his family were in Visegrad in May, June. This prompted me to say that I knew him and to state that he was in Visegrad throughout that time." The Defence take issue with the fact that she couldn't recall whether she saw him specifically on the 27th or 28th of June. The fact is, she said he and his family were living in Visegrad up until the day she left, and the day she left was the 29th of June. The Sredoje Lukic Defence offers a number of arguments that the evidence of VG-035 is unreliable. None of these arguments is persuasive. First, the Sredoje Lukic Defence suggests that VG-035 marked the wrong location when asked to mark the Meho Aljic house on a photograph. The Chamber will recall from Ms. Turjacanin's testimony that the Meho Aljic house was immediately behind the Sadikovic house. The Alic house is no longer there, so he was asking the witness to mark a spot on the ground where a house once stood in a picture taken from several hundred feet up in the air. If the Chamber examines P101 and P102, it will be clear that VG-035 marked the open area immediately next to the Sadikovic house, simply on the west side of the house instead of the south side of the house; I submit, a completely insignificant error given the passage of 16 years, the absence ever the Aljic house, and the fact that the witness was being asked to mark an aerial photograph, a type of evidence that often causes confusion with witnesses. The Sredoje Lukic Defence has also attempted to impugn VG-035's evidence by making erroneous statements about the effect of Court Witness 002's evidence. VG-035 and Court Witness 002 were together on the morning of the Bikavac fire when Milan and Sredoje Lukic entered their home. VG-035 identified both accused as being there, while Court Witness 002 only recognised Milan Lukic. The Defence state that Court Witness 002 knew Sredoje Lukic because he used to rent an apartment in her house, and, therefore, the fact that she did not recognise him as the second man contradicts VG-035's evidence. This assertion misstates Court Witness 002's evidence. Court Witness 002 stated that Sredoje Lukic lived in the house before she married into the family. She never said that she knew him, and there is no reason to assume that she did. The Sredoje Lukic Defence declined to ask her any questions when it was offered, saying at transcript page 7084: "This has nothing to do with our particular case." They certainly could have inquired whether she knew Sredoje Lukic, but did not. The only evidence in this trial is that she knew Sredoje Lukic lived in the house she moved into before she married her husband and moved into that house. While such a statement may suggest her husband may have known him, it does not suggest in any interpretation, however broad, that she knew Sredoje Lukic herself. In our initial review of the Milan Lukic final trial brief, we have found it often misstates evidence. The time constraints we are working under today do not permit a comprehensive listing of these misstatements. The Prosecution will therefore list just an example or two. One of these misstatements relates to VG-035. In paragraph 113 of their brief, the Milan Lukic Defence asserts that VG-035 testified "... as to a blond Milan Lukic being the one that committed crimes she testified about." This is a misstatement of the evidence. During her testimony in precisely the very pages cited by the Defence, VG-035 said that Milan Lukic had dark brown hair. That's at transcripts page 1719. In addition, in her statement, which the Defence also cites as Exhibit 1D44, she also clearly stated that Milan Lukic had "dark brown, short hair." One point with respect to hair colour: The Defence make the point that there are differences in how witnesses have described the hair colour of Milan Lukic. Please don't overlook the evidence of VG-142, the Serbian official who interviewed him as found on page 4 of his statement in evidence of P144. VG-142 recalled in that statement that when they arrested Milan Lukic, when he came to him, he had a fur cap that Milan Lukic described as a traditional Chetnik cap. He went on to describe how Milan Lukic had some of his hair highlighted. VG-142 thought it looked ridiculous and asked Milan Lukic about it, and he said that it was a whim of his girlfriend. You will also recall VG-094's evidence that on the day Milan Lukic stopped her family in the Visegrad square, one of the people in Milan Lukic's car was a woman she recognised as a hairdresser in the town. There is credible evidence before the Chamber that Milan Lukic was, for whatever reason, colouring his hair at the time. I submit variations between witnesses seeing him at different times regarding his hair colour may also be due to his dying his hair during this period. The Sredoje Lukic Defence makes a great deal about the fact that Huso's father Hasib did not mention Sredoje as a perpetrator of the Pionirska fire during his video-taped interview in July 1992. Hasib was not reunited with Huso until January of 1993, but they then discussed the events and perpetrators a number of times. Hasib was clear that Sredoje, who he knew well, was one of the main Pionirska perpetrators, and he left his son Huso the solemn task of telling what happened at Pionirska Street. Why he did not mention Sredoje Lukic's name in the interview some days after the fire? Recall Huso Kurspahic's evidence that he destroyed his reports about the fire in 1993 because he feared the Bosnian Serbs would get them. He believed they would know who had identified perpetrators in Visegrad, and this would endanger those people. When Hasib gave that statement, he had just fled Visegrad knowing that the Lukic group was actively trying to find him and kill him. Although Hasib is not here to tell us why he didn't mention them by name, it is reasonable to infer that he did not do so because he was afraid. As soon as he was safely with his son, he gave his son a full list of the people who perpetrated the fire. There is no reasonable explanation as to why Hasib would later fabricate Sredoje's involvement in the crime when he knew him so well and was so friendly with him. Throughout their submissions, the Defence have implicitly asked the Trial Chamber to analyse the evidence in this case in a highly artificial manner. Specifically, the Defence have asked the Chamber to look at the evidence of each witness in isolation and ask itself whether the evidence of that one witness, standing alone, is sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. The Defence prefer this artificial method of analysis because it allows them to avoid the fact that these witnesses, separated from the day of the crimes in most cases, corroborate and reinforce each other's evidence. The Prosecution evidence when examined in its entirety clearly establishes the guilt of the two accused. The Chamber must analyse each element of the evidence in this case in light of the trial record as a whole. The totality of evidence in this case paints a picture of the events upon which the indictment is based, and this picture is clear and certain when all of the evidence is viewed together. The Limaj Appeals Chamber cited approvingly a lesson from the Limaj Trial Chamber: "It is the cumulative effect of the evidence, i.e., the totality of the evidence bearing on the identification of an accused, which must be weighed to determine whether the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that each accused is a perpetrator as alleged." When all of the evidence in this case it considered in its totality, its cumulative effect is a clear and compelling picture of the crimes perpetrated by both accused. Both briefs suggest that the Prosecution witnesses are lying about who the perpetrators were while failing to explain what possible motive they could have to lie. We have seen time and time again during this trial the extraordinary character of the women of Visegrad; women who endured unspeakable crimes so that their children might survive; women whose quick thinking and strength saved their children; and women whose last act on this earth was a failed attempt to protect their children from the flames. These women of incredible strength and integrity literally tempered by fire did not come to this Tribunal to falsely accuse anyone. They came before you and testified about the people they recognised, and they candidly admitted that there were some perpetrators who they simply did not know.
