Not only has there been no demonstrated motive for them to fabricate anything, but there has been compelling evidence that where there may have been a motive to fabricate, none succumb to it. The survivors of Pionirska spoke about their life-long neighbours forcing them from their homes, ransacking their possessions before their very eyes. In their minds, these are the people who began the ordeal that cost them so very much. Yet despite this, none of the survivors placed these people at the fire. None of them suggest they had any direct involvement in the fire. I submit that this is proof that they have not fabricated anything. If they were inclined to fabricate who the perpetrators were, they would have placed these people there and not Milan and certainly not Sredoje Lukic, someone they had no animosity toward, but actually had affection for. They have placed Sredoje and Milan Lukic there because they were there. Even those who died in the fire, the question arises again, why would they say it was the Lukics who were there if it was not true? The voices of the victims who died in Pionirska Street fire speak loudly and credibly through those that survived, yet the Defence maintain that you cannot rely on these witnesses. I did not choose these witnesses; fate chose them. Perhaps there were other people in the Pionirska or Bikavac fires with better memories, better eyesight, people who could have told you the precise height and weight of each of the perpetrators. Fate chose the survivors, not the Prosecution. My duty as an international Prosecutor is to bring those who survived and their evidence before you, and although it presents far greater challenges than in a domestic criminal trial, I don't ask for any diminishment of my burden to prove the guilt of these two men beyond a reasonable doubt. These witnesses also present special challenges for you who will have to adjudicate this case. Some of these witnesses by their own admission have limited education, are sometimes confused on minor details. Some are irreparably traumatised, and their trauma is still obvious to us 16 years later. But that is not, as is suggested, a reason to dismiss their evidence. You as international criminal judges were selected especially to adjudicate these cases and have the experience necessary to discern the truth, to evaluate the evidence from witnesses still suffering the effects of terrible crimes. If you acquit one or both of the accused, you must do so not because of who they are, not because of their palpable brokenness. If you acquit one or both of the accused, it must only be because you come to the conclusion that you do not believe them. And I submit that a careful analysis of their evidence, the lack of any reason for them to fabricate their account, the personal cost testifying has exacted on them, when you take everything into consideration, the only conclusion possible is that their evidence establishes the guilt of both accused. In keeping with the conduct of the Milan Lukic Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. In keeping with the conduct of the Milan Lukic Defence over the course of this trial, their brief makes miriad of unsubstantiated allegations against the Prosecution and myself in particular. This is in keeping with the pattern of similar conduct over the course of the trial in which not only the Prosecution, but the Trial Chamber, the Registrar, the governments of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia have all at some point had serious allegations cavalierly thrown at them. I regret that they have enjoyed the freedom to do this. It is now five months since I filed a request before the Chamber requesting that the Milan Lukic Defence be directed to either substantiate their allegations or withdraw them. I will not devote any time to these allegations now other than to say that despite the Chamber granting the Milan Lukic Defence every opportunity to investigate and substantiate their claims, granting nearly every request they made for information, for contact details of people they believed would prove their spurious claims, none of these people have been called to testify. One of them was VG-031. I cited simply as one of several examples. Despite the allegations regarding him, despite being given the opportunity to call him, they now claim in their brief that the Chamber denied them the ability to call him as a witness, something clearly contradicted by the Chamber's decision of the 13th of March, 2009, allowing him to be called. But he wasn't called, and somehow others are to blame. The end result has been that the Defence has chosen not to call any evidence substantiating any of the allegations they made against the Prosecution, against the Chamber, against the Registrar, and against Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. In fact, the only evidence of impropriety during this trial is against Milan Lukic and his Defence team, some of which came from a former Defence witness himself. I expect the Milan Lukic Defence closing will follow their opening, a long litany of slanderous, unsubstantiated statements. I will have no opportunity to reply. I ask the Chamber to insist that any allegations be supported by evidence. Do not let this Chamber be misused as a platform for slander. As I conclude my remarks, I would like to thank the witnesses and their families. I know that for most, their testimony here re-opened deep wounds. Their willingness to revisit these painful memories was an essential contribution to the truth. In particular, I would like to thank those women who described vicious, terrible attacks knowing that this Chamber would not be considering charges related to those attacks. I would also like to thank the government of Serbia who provided relevant evidence it had in its possession and made available a government official to testify. I would also like to thank the current police in Visegrad who on several occasions facilitated visits to the crime scenes by myself and my staff. I hope that such cooperation is a sign that the Visegrad police is once again a professional organisation protecting the legal rights of all Visegrad citizens. I hope both of these examples of cooperation are evidence that the Tribunal is realising its goal of fostering reconciliation in the region. In my final few minutes, I would like to address you on the issue of sentence. There is a line from Khaled Hosseini's book The Kite Runner that says: "There's only one sin, only one, and that is theft. Every other sin is a variation of theft. When you kill a man, you steal a life. You steal his wife's right to a husband, rob his children of a father." Viewed in those terms, it's incalculable what the two accused have taken from Visegrad. The magnitude of their theft can never be calculated. We will never know how Meliha Memisevic's life changed the day she watched Milan Lukic murder her father in cold blood. We will never know what would have become of the 2-day-old infant burned alive in the Pionirska fire. She would now be looking forward to her 17th birthday in a few weeks. We will never know the contributions she would have made to her community, to our world. What they stole from the individual families, from the Visegrad community, from us as a human race cannot be ascertained. Someone once posed a question to me whether I ever calculated the years of human lives taken in the Pionirska and Bikavac fires. How many years of human life were taken? It is a surprisingly simple yet stark calculation to make. The average life expectancy of a person in the former Yugoslavia is over 70 years. Hajra Kurspahic was 60 years old when she die d in Pionirska. Ten years of her life were taken. Most of the Bikavac victims we know nothing about other than Ms. Turjacanin's recollection that the Aljic house was filled mostly with young mothers and children. But only considering the victims of the two fires we know and have evidence about their age, just considering them alone, the number is staggering: Over 3.000 years of human life lost in those two fires. What the two accused destroyed in June of 1992 is far beyond their capacity to repay. Spending the remainder of their lives incarcerated is simply a nominal token toward the loss they occasioned. Criminal theorists have long considered that one of the important functions of punishment is general deterrence; sending a message to potential offenders to deter them should they consider perpetrating similar crimes. If you find the accused guilty for the Pionirska or Bikavac fires or both, I ask the Court to seize the opportunity to send a clear, unequivocal message to those who might consider similarly egregious crimes, those who are apt to similarly exploit the vulnerable and in the chaos of conflict. Use your judgement and sentence to make clear three things: One, if you perpetrate crimes like this, you will be pursued and you will be found. You will be extradited from your hiding place and brought to a court where you will be held accountable; two, you will be tried fairly, no matter your conduct, no matter how the seriousness of the allegations against you. You will have a full and a fair trial; and three, if you are found guilty of such crimes against the world's most vulnerable, no mercy will be shown. You will be given the severest of sentences. There must be no question of the International Community's resolve to vigorously pursue and hold responsible those who commit crimes such as these during the conflict. If this Chamber finds the accused guilty of the Pionirska and Bikavac fires, the Prosecution recommends that it hand down a sentence that ensures that the accused spend the remainder of their lives incarcerated, the most severe sentence within your power. Your Honours, my work on this case is now concluded. The Prosecution has fairly laid before you all of the evidence available related to the indictment against Sredoje and Milan Lukic. Every person who survived these crimes and is still alive has been brought before you. In addition, all other witnesses with relevant evidence have also testified. You now have it all for your consideration. The evidence clearly and compellingly establishes the culpability of both Sredoje and Milan Lukic beyond reasonable doubt. It is now for the Chamber to carefully consider it and adjudicate the indictment against them. I wish the Chamber wisdom in this important task. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think as Mr. Groome said, this has been a long and arduous road we started. I'd first like to thank the Chamber for being patient with my ignorance of the procedures and the nuance of this Chamber. I'd like to thank all the court staff and everyone who has put up with my level of disorganisation and lack of functionality in this arena. And I'd even like to thank the Prosecution; although we've seen -- not always seen eye to eye, I believe that there has been a high level of disclosure, albeit in mass quantities at times. I've been impressed by the levels of candour at times that has come through the pleadings, even though frustrated the ability to present it under the restraints of the court. I'd like to start off my closing submissions, Your Honour, with some quotations that mean a little bit to me and kind of mean a little bit to me in hopes of looking at this case and taking tongue and cheek a little bit, but in taking a quote from Eleanor Roosevelt which I felt resonated with me, is: "Do what you feel in your heart to be right, and you'll be criticized any way. You'll be dammed if you do and dammed if you don't." That's important, Your Honour, because I think that that resonates both with the choices I've made in handling this case as well as the difficult decisions that you have before you as a concerted group of people that has the most difficult demanding sorting-throughs of the facts that I can imagine. And although this case was relegated to a level 1, not knowing the difference, I think this is the most difficult of cases. I quote to Longfellow because: "If we could read the secret history of our enemies, we should find in each person's life sorrow and suffering enough to disarm all hostility." I think that's important because unless you really look at all of these people and their in their gentlest, in their difficulties, in their where they come from, it's very difficult for us especially in the first world to relate to them. And I think that none of us have had the sorrow to have gone through what all of these people went through. It's a point of which I've only begun to scratch the surface with myself. And I take a quote from Bridge Over the Drina, because I think it really goes to what's happened in this case, upon my opinion, and that's: "The common people remember and tell of what they are able to grasp and what they are able to transform into legend." I think that's important because all of these ordinary and simple folks of which I lump Mr. Lukic into have a very limited set of sophistication of which to approach, I think, the big picture in this case. And I quote Mr. Marley only because this has been a hard-fought fight, and I believe that what I have been doing in honour is to uphold the rights of Mr. Lukic despite the allegations which when I first met this case, Your Honour, were horrendous. When I first read the articles about Mr. Lukic, I shuddered and I wondered what I was doing getting on a plane to come over here. And with regards to that, though, I'm proud of the job we've done, and I wish we could have done more. I cite to Judge Hunt and his trepidations about the completion strategy simply because I think that that was part of this case. It's a necessary evil that has made it difficult at times to prosecute every angle, as Mr. Groome stated, and I wish I had had more time. I cite to Judge Wald because, with all due respect to the Chamber, we had a discourse many months ago, Judge Van den Wyngaert, where you said I'm not a jury, and I'd like to think that we all are. The minute the evidence closes and you go back in there and you've made your decisions as judges, you've decided what's in and what's out, and when you go back there, I ask that you simply look at all the evidence, and let's decide whether or not there's reasonable doubt. Even if you think Mr. Lukic is guilty of something, the important thing is did the Prosecution prove beyond a reasonable doubt what they did in these indictments, not everything else. I'm using this, this is something I use in jury trials back home, and I don't mean to offend the intelligence of the Court, only that this is illustrative of how difficult the burden beyond a reasonable doubt is, how lofty a principle it is that set such a high bar on the Prosecution. And with all due respect to the Prosecution, I feel that at best they've presented here is a preponderance of the evidence case, where we can actually flip the coin maybe and decide whether Mr. Lukic is guilty or not. But reasonable doubt isn't of itself according to the uniform jury instruction of my jurisdiction which is proof so convincing that you would rely on it without hesitation in the most important of your own affairs. That's a tough one because even though we can be pretty darn sure, especially with all the spurious allegations that are tangential to Mr. Lukic's case, it is still beyond-a-reasonable-doubt of evidence that we must apply to these counts. I ask you to reverse roles with everyone, and I do this in respect to Mr. Jerry Spence who I work with back in the States, is his method of teaching trial skills is that the lawyers must explore their case, explore their witnesses, explore their clients by doing as much as internal soul-searching as possible, as much internal psychodrama of which we can stand to try and get into the skin of the players of our case and hopefully find the truth. This is a little bit of edification of what we believe the OTP has put at us constant levelling of accusations of malfeasance against us. They've thrown unindicted cases at you which we believe were unsubstantiated, and we believe that the OTP has treated this Court very much like a jury, attempting to sway its opinion, not based on the quality of the evidence, but about the quantity of the accusations. I believe this is how the OTP wants you simply to see my client and Mr. Cepic's client. They want you to see him in this sterile courtroom, this environment that whether or not we put it on paper what the standard is, there is very much an appearance and a feeling of guilt if you sit in those chairs. There is absolutely nothing like being accused, and if you could find some place in your own lives where you've been falsely accused of something, maybe inconsequential in the grand scheme of things, but make yourself remember how you that made you feel, and you'll only begin to understand. You know, this case has transformed over time, and the Prosecution has changed the way they've presented their case because at the beginning you would have sworn -- and by the indictments that have been handed down out of Visegrad, you would swear that Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and Sredoje Lukic were the architects of Visegrad, that no one else was doing anything bad in town but these guys, and yet where are the leaders of Visegrad? Where is Savovic? Where is Perisic? The Court issued subpoenas. They were not responded to. So in thanking the government of Serbia, I wonder if they did everything they could to make sure these witnesses came here. I think it's important because the Prosecution has been back-pedalling on their presentation as to the level of authority and/or control that Milan Lukic had, much less now Sredoje Lukic as a last-ditch attempt to save their case. I ask you to look at this in the portens, and I'll try not to go, is why a site visit would have been good. You've seen the overhead of Bikavac so many times, Your Honour, and I can't tell you enough how misleading that aerial photo is. Bikavac is a hill-side neighbourhood, and yet in all the photographs it appears to be a pastoral valley. It's actually -- the entire town, I think to get a sense of the layout is important for understanding the nature of the allegations. So I start here with a map, a precise and military map, showing Rujiste and marked up through one of our witnesses, and at the 22 kilometres, anyone that wanted to go to Rujiste to Visegrad, half of that would be on a dirt road. Half of it is above snow line, and I would actually address this to Judge David only in so much that he remembers the mountains of New Mexico, the north of near Chama and Brazos. You go to Visegrad, and you will see this kind of place, and the people are similar. They are ethnically segregated. They are humble, and yet they are fiercely loyal. These people remind me of northern New Mexico, and their country mirrors it almost exactly. And so I came, and it was only until I saw this places that I sort of understood them a little bit if you've ever been to Mora and you try to go into the grocery store and you're not from there and you don't speak Spanish, you may not get served. These people are insular and insulated in a similar way. This case is about, for me, the son of Mile and Kata, born the 6th of September, 1967, in Rujiste municipality. I ask you decide whether he is a war criminal or a scapegoat, a leader or a follower. To me, Milan from Rujiste is that little boy in the middle of his mother and his sister Dragina. He is the gentleman with always an arm around him or an arm around someone else. In every photograph we showed you of him as a young up-and-coming man, all the way up until the war, shows him as a gregarious, smiling, social person. I look at -- ask you to look at the pictures below because that is Rujiste, and I took that snowy photo myself, standing in the plum orchard that is circled on the map. You see those dots in that yellow map, Your Honour? Well, that is Rujiste, and that is Milan's home, and MLD lived just across those lines. The person that would testify for Milan Lukic, MLD10, lived there, and so is it really hard to believe, and why does bribery have to become involved, when someone who has been your neighbour in the mountains your whole life that you've dealt with the trials and tribulations of living outside of town together would in fact ally themselves in times of chaos? Before the war, Milan Lukic was a brother, a teenager, a student, a young man, a clown, a bartender; and when the powers turned on chaos, he became a police officer, a soldier, now a fugitive, and an accused war criminal. But he also became a father in that time. And I ask you, if you look in these photographs, do you see someone that could do exactly what they're saying, at least without the most careful of circumspection. I ask you to look at the photograph in the middle with the two gentlemen and everyone with their bad antiquated hair-cuts, but those are the Muslim boys that were his best friends identified by MLD-10. This is a boy that was raised in a mixed community. You cannot take the accusations of the Prosecution lightly, and we will discuss the motives, that fabricate that we have. 1D14, Milan Lukic just a few months before the war, Your Honour. This is the guy that journalists would call the warlord of Visegrad. I see him as being an ordinary man who, if you had looked at this, you would never, ever think he would be an internationally accused war criminal at some point in his life. We brought Dr. Hough, and clearly, his qualifications and his demeanour resonated with the Prosecution because they sided to him and his reasoning when it supports their position. Well, I'd say if you give him the credibility to do that, then we must also give him the credibility to assess Milan Lukic, I think with a role that is also been shown by the rest of the evidence. This is important, Your Honour. In my jurisdiction, the case would be dismissed based on an affidavit or arrest warrant that included such diametrically opposed descriptions of the suspect of the crimes. In the international warrant to INTERPOL, it cited blue eyes, eagle tattoos, and a mole. I apologise for the issue with regards to the blond hair cited by Mr. Groome, but actually it was the blue eyes, and we just -- for whatever reason, blond hair he escaped in there, but it was blue eyes. It was the most important thing that you cannot take away. I'd like to address the Drina River first because I think from a practical perspective, as a criminal Defence lawyer, the Drina River is the most difficult for you to determine. It's the most difficult because you have on your plate two eye-witness survivors that say my client's there shooting them. You also have a former accused who testified in his own trial that my client shot at those people. That's a lot on your plate, and I admit that, and I'd like to hopefully prove to you why there is doubt still despite that feeling of being overwhelmed. First things first is ID. ID is up in the air as it's concerned to VG-014 and 32. It's up in the air. It's not resolved. There are serious inconsistencies between the eye-witnesses, especially if you include VG-079 into the equation, and the OTP has failed to account for the self-serving nature and unrebutted by cross-examination the Defence of Mitar Vasiljevic. See, he put on a Defence of which no one representing Milan was there to cross-examine him on those tough questions, so of course he wanted completely to mitigate his role, and that needs to be explored because he hoped to walk out of this courtroom acquitted, and he didn't. And the OTP has failed to rebut beyond a reasonable doubt the alibi evidence presented by Milan Lukic. I won't get into the thing. These are just simply quotes out of our final brief, but it goes to the fact that VG-14 centred his identification of Milan Lukic around a mole. So let's look at this. I put all four photographs unretouched and marked by VG-14 an VG-032, and if you -- they were asked in a pinch to circle what they thought was the mole that was being referred to, and if you look at the unmarked versus the marked, there's nothing there. More importantly, Your Honours, there's nothing there that would be of the magnitude that if you put soot or black paint on your face, that these kind of moles would not simply disappear under the covering. I show this because this has been the vanted OTP photograph of Milan Lukic, the supposed White Eagle. Isn't it just as likely it's a souvenir photograph because I've seen this hat on other heads, and how can we say it's not even the same one? But the most important thing we take from this, Your Honour, is here's a photograph that shows no mole that can be misinterpreted by any witness, and I think it's arguable that this is the issue. Still skeptical? Where was the mole? Let's look at a bunch of other photographs of his face over time and see if that circle on the side of his face is a botched mole removal, and I don't think we have anything here to show that there is such a thing. Now, this is interesting because VG-014 has two ways of knowing Milan Lukic. One is this mole and this personal thing, but then he says he also interacts with him during the two years that he went to school. Well, arguably, Your Honour, you have in your custody the school records of Milan Lukic, and he went to school for the full time. So that's wrong. VG-014's wrong. He went to him with the school the entire time, but why was that explainable? They weren't in the same section. So they didn't see each other and go to class together. They saw each other. And what did he know about the Milan Lukic that went to school with him? He was a boy that never got into fights with people of Muslim origins. He was soft-spoken, and he took the time to say hi to VG-014. Is that someone we would expect to be a future war criminal? Really? So I point your attention to Novica Lukic, Milan Lukic's older brother. Now, we're not saying that Novica Lukic is a suspect, but if I were a person maybe talking with a friend of mine, maybe VG-014 talking to VG-032 and they're trying to figure out who just tried to, and they could see a mole but couldn't tell who else it was, they might remember a Lukic with a mole. As if we talked about memory with Dr. LaGrange, certain things when we believe it or we say it can become parts of our reality, and then it doesn't matter anymore. But he was a person with the Lukic last name with a noticeable mole on his face as opposed to Milan Lukic, and there's even Milan there as a younger and medium age right next to him that we can look at and see that there is no mole. VG-032, he had never, ever had the time to know Milan Lukic and only gained this knowledge through hearsay at the end. This is an important diagram because it gets into the eye-witness testimony, and it corroborates and deals with the eye-witness testimony of VG-079 who was across the river with binoculars. This is important. In the original statements of VG-079, he documented a Paglicija, not a Passat. Regardless of whether or not the Passat was there is an issue of credibility of these witnesses, and why does VG-014 and VG-032 have reason to do this? Because it's easy for them to lie if the only nexus they had between the accused was a Passat. It's too easy for them never having to know Milan Lukic and simply because everyone saw him at the Passat at some point in time. That is not -- that would be dispositive maybe if VG-079 wasn't across the river seeing a very different car which I would argue could not in any stretch of the imagination be misconstrued for a Passat, and -- 4-door versus 2-door. And more importantly, VG-079 with the aid of his binoculars without needing to speak to other people was able to identify two of the named victims at the river. That means that the binoculars, if they are good enough to ID a person, they're good enough to ID a car. They're good enough to ID colours of uniforms. They're good enough to ID headwear. And what you have is VG-079 in the very beginning documented black uniforms; not just black face, black uniforms, black hats, black scarves, skulls on them. That is absolutely diametrically opposed to a blue beret and blue -- especially if I can recognise my friends. Again, this is a slide related to that. I did this for illustration, the reason being is is that the witness identified that little white car in the background as a Jugo, and that's right, and I think we've all seen those tiny cars that are made by the former Yugoslavia. And in looking at this photograph, it is important because, albeit cramped, you can fit ten people in these two cars. You can barely fit ten people. That's three in the back of each and two in the front of each. One person has to be very, very uncomfortable if you add an extra soldier. VG-079 in his original statements said ten: Seven individuals, three soldiers dressed in black. It's only in this trial have they added a fourth soldier, and only in this trial is the uniform changing. Mitar Vasiljevic, he seems to be the crux. He came in here, he swore under oath, and he basically sent his kum down the river. He testified on his own behalf in his own trial. He gave an OTP statement in his own trial, and during that time, he presented himself in the most out-of-the-picture sort of way, saying he was hiding, he didn't have a gun, and all these things, and you know what his Trial Chamber did? They chose to believe him that he was there but not believe him that he was not involved. Why? Because VG-014 and VG-032 identified him. They recognised him. This is a perfect example of the difference between knowing somebody and not because --

utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- you can't say VG-014 didn't know Mitar. Of course he knew Mitar. They drank together --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- as did Mitar with half the town. Why? Because he was the biggest drunk in town, and we want to make him the architects of these killings. Dr. LaGrange testified that based on the history presented to her regarding his alcoholism, his drinking, his bingeing, his blackouts, it was likely that he had some brain damage. It's likely that that brain damage affected memory, but more importantly, you also got to consider state-dependent memory, Your Honour, because the day before this, Mitar Vasiljevic buried his nephew. He had been drinking, certainly, and he was drinking the next day by his own admission. If he was drunk at the time, he needs to be drunk again to remember. That is state-dependent memory. Just have one slide dedicated to Uzamnica, and that is simply this, that in the earlier statements before the Court, there are very limited references to Milan Lukic supposedly entering the jail and doing things that we would say he shouldn't be doing as a caretaker of anybody in custody. However, if you look at their subsequent statements and, worse than that, the statements as the OTP is speaking to them, the instances become greatly exaggerated, and so we need to explore why these witnesses need to go from one or two times coming in to every day, and that is about how much the stakes go up. The Koric killing. We don't have much on that, Your Honour. We have two witnesses, VG-035 and CW-2. The issue with VG-035 is this, and that was I think the problem with the OTP is that he had birth marks and blue eyes. That's who she identified as him. She believed that the OTP her showed a photospread with both Sredoje and Milan, but she identified them in court. There was no photo arrays given by the Prosecution, and that she is a member and her statement was prepared by Bakira Hasecic in her organisation, and that her statement was then sent to the ICTY. CW-002 also confirmed that the Milan Lukic she believed had blond hair, that's where we mixed that up. Milan's brother lived with her husband, and changed her story about who shot Hajra Koric and dropped by Prosecution as a witness. Also, her statement was prepared by Bakira's association. The Varda factory. The OTP failed to establish beyond a reasonable doubt the ID of Milan Lukic. Why? Because they took all the witnesses that were so far away. Again, the ID is based solely on the Passat and not about an actual identification of Milan Lukic. They failed to rebut beyond a reasonable doubt the alibi evidence. They failed to establish beyond a reasonable doubt the identity of the alleged victims. Why? As we filed the bar table, two of those alleged victims were reported dead on different days. Two of the people are asking for their property back. This is an issue where the identity of these people is still up in the air much less how, why, when, and where they passed away. Look at this place, Your Honour. Look at the screen. Look how big this factory is. This is a huge factory. Now we have the multiple drawings of the witnesses, and where are the witnesses that supposedly identify in P190, a good distance away from the guard shack, either up on the balcony of the house or in a chicken coop, all several hundred metres away. This takes me back home because I think of myself, and we always have immigration raids around where I live, and when they go into the factories they usually cordon off all the exits and then round up people and take them and ship them off. In the first statements of the witness presented by the Office of the Prosecutor, Milan Lukic went in there by himself. He went into this complex and brought out seven named guys, took them out, and then one of the witness's statements actually separated them, walked all the way down to the river, shot three guys, come back up, get the other four who - God knows why they'd wait around - and take them back down and shoot them too. Again, all from the vantage point of this 200-metres-away situation, all based on a supposed red Passat there and nothing else. VG-031, we were chastised by the Prosecution today saying that I'd dropped the ball. Your Honour, we filed our motion with regards to VG-031 the 1st of December. It was not ruled upon as permission to allow us to call him until March 13th, nearly the end of trial, and the Court did not order the Prosecution to give his contact information until March 30th. That was too late. We believe that the statement stands on its own, and from a perspective of reasonable doubt, Your Honour, it's big because when you have a worker inside that can name two of the victims as being with two other named recognised by-name Serbs, at a distance, and then he gives the Prosecution three other names that say they saw the same thing I did, at the very least it would start to make sense to me that it would take more than one guy to cordon off a factory that big. But here's why I don't believe Milan Lukic has been proven to be there. It's because the same way the water cooler works, you mean to tell me this guy VG-031 wouldn't have heard Milan Lukic is there? It's okay that he didn't see the thing by the river. It's okay that he only saw the two other guys. But you sure would think that he would mention to investigators what he saw. These, again, are the death certificates that are the subject of our most recent bar table, with two of the members most notably Mr. Velagic who is reported to have died May 30th of 1992, not 10 of June, 1992; and Mr. Memisevic is alleged to have died the 9th of June, although we could argue that that's, yes, close enough, but one is way out of the way. Our expert, former deputy chief of police of Albuquerque, New Mexico Clifford Jenkins stated that: Given the overall quality of the Varda investigation, I would want my investigators to do more before I brought it to the Prosecution. Pionirska. This is a big one because I think it brought the most witnesses, probably the most notoriety. We believe the Prosecution has failed wholeheartedly. The OTP failed to establish beyond a reasonable doubt the ID of Milan Lukic as being involved. They are asking for life based on the evidence and the strength of the evidence that they're asking in this case. They didn't even establish beyond a reasonable doubt, Your Honour, the identity of the actual victims. Instead, they attempt to amend their list as we prove people are alive, as we prove that witnesses lied about not seeing them. They lied about seeing them at funerals. They failed the correct, and yet if you take a murderer case in its simplest, usually one person killing one person, I'm sorry; if the body shows up alive, the case is dismissed. There's a notorious case in the United States where a gentleman dilled his wife and his in-laws and then tried to kill himself, but he set the house on fire and burned his victims alive. Imagine if three of those supposed victims showed up in Mexico sometime later. What would happen to the case even if we thought he killed one person? Pionirska Street is important. This is just to demonstrate that. This is the power, if you will, of the Prosecution's case. These beautiful people, these beautiful people that are unaccounted for but yet, wait, some of them are accounted for. Some are living and had already left and yet were reported deceased by these witnesses, maybe attempting to find justice for unindicted or silent alleged victims. This is important. This is from the Prosecution's PowerPoint of their opening. This shows the Hotel Visegrad of which -- where all these bad guys were supposed to be staying, and it shows the way that the Kurspahic family and others had come down from their home village and then ended up in the Mahala neighbourhood. This shows that the Prosecution has changed their story, and I didn't have time to go back to the Vasiljevic exhibits that maybe led to this, but as you can see, Your Honour, this diagram actually shows people going through an opposite pathway to the Omeragic house. It is not the same as the witnesses later dictated. As you can see, the yellow line goes behind and between these Memic houses, and, in fact, in the most recent testimony, the Memic house changes. This, the Prosecution accuses us of misleading. Look at this exhibit that was in their final brief. I don't know what these headlights are. I don't know where that came from. I don't know. It's uncited to the transcript, but if you look at the Exhibits that were there, if you look at P057 in the bottom right-hand corner to this, I recall specific testimony that there were some lights, ambient light from the houses all the way across the creek-bed where the people escaped to. But here is more important to this, Your Honour. If you look down there, the shed to which VG-078 and VG-101 hid in, really? One, I don't remember that evidence coming in anywhere, and then if you look at the P57, there's that shed at the top of the far side of the hill, which means these people while escaping got to go up the draw, through the underbrush, which would make a lot of noise and a whole different thing to go up to the other side. I don't believe that was the evidence. I believe they are looking at this picture thinking, well, that looks like it's in the bottom of the draw. But clearly, you can say it's 50 feet higher than the bottom. This is it. VG-115. Supposedly she saved herself by saying, oh, she could see smoke and fire from her vantage point on the balcony of where we took the pictures. Well, one, this is where it documents this change where in fact that the lines drawn by all the witnesses don't go around the back of that house or the front of the house, but more importantly, this, Your Honour, if you look at one of those lines, one of those lines is VG-115 saying Mitar Vasiljevic is on a white horse, riding with a cast, yelling at these poor victims to get in the house. VG-115 was shown to be not credible by the Trial Chamber and the Vasiljevic Appeals Chamber based on her testimony before that case, and if you want to take a white horse and a guy in a cast doing this, the town drunk, that is where it gets crazy. They brought up the issue that this was somehow some air fuel. Why? Because one of the VG witnesses said that the carpet was so soaked with kerosene that now the theory becomes but the air just exploded and blew everybody up. The problem is, as Mr. O'Donnell stated, an expert with explosives, is were there a enough of the fumes to do that, there wouldn't be any survivors. There wouldn't have been people coming out of the windows. This place would have been rocked, and there would have been no one crying or screaming or getting shot for an half an hour. Important about Mr. O'Donnell, Your Honours, is simply this, and it's a theory of the case that I believe is true: If something happened at Pionirska, I think that to call everyone mistaken or absolutely crazy is not the way it happened. I believe they couldn't ID Milan Lukic if their life depended on it, and that's really the way it was. They didn't know him. They didn't have the reasons, and their tendrils of identification are so closely related to Mitar Vasiljevic who could not have been there. He broke his leg. So everyone that said they saw Mitar is lying. Why? Because they all knew Mitar. It wasn't a issue of maybe it's him. They all knew him, drank with him, or saw him at the local restaurant. The important thing about my theory, though, is that for there to be shrapnel in the wall from whatever was thrown in there to hurt these good people, there cannot be 60 people packed in that tiny room because then those 60 people would absorb and there would be no pathways to the walls. The only reason for that shrapnel to make it to the wall is if there was at least few enough that there is spacing to allow that. This room I believe if anything, if there was a fire, if there was a flash, if there was anything, it was a grenade. It was some small improvised explosive device. Did it catch someone's skirt on fire or something to give a witness that? Maybe. But if you went there and did a site visit, you would see a dank, mouldy, wet environment, and that flooring, if you soaked the floor-boards with it would be gone. It would be burnt. All of our experts basically prove that regardless of what happened 15, 16 years ago in that basement room of Pionirska, it was not a fully involved room fire. There's not the evidence. So if you believe in part the witnesses for the Prosecution, it is possible they are simply mistaken. Why? They escaped. But the biggest proof that goes towards my theory, Your Honour, is that they heard voices and shots for that half an hour. I think we all can imagine if the fire was -- enveloped everyone, you would not hear the screams. Officer Jenkins stated simply that all of this evidence speaks directly to whether or not the possibility the crime even occurred, and I would argue, in the manner it's described. I believe that this case is completely about rape. I believe that this case is about sons that did not come home on individual arrests. I believe this case is about someone that you believe did something and you're willing to seek justice even if it's not the right count.

utterances.text: Three young teenagers were alleged to have been kidnapped by Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. They were alleged to be driven to the bridge. They were -- two of them were alleged to be thrown off and shot in the water in cold blood while two non-descript soldiers sat in the back. Former case manager Marie O'Leary took off a cartoon clip art of three young boys that I had on there to illustrate how silly the story is of four soldiers, all their armaments, and three 14-year-old boys having to squeeze between the two in the back with a sniper barrel in their face, yet the witness had no clear recollection of the entry and exit to the vehicle. That is important because if you go look at any Passat, we were going to try to find one and squeeze a bunch of people into it put it on video, but it's a ridiculous, ridiculous assumption unless the witness accounts for such an uncomfortable situation. And then for this witness to have witnessed two murders of his friends and then be taken to the jail and then let go as if nothing had happened, it's an illogical story meant simply to establish an alibi rebuttal without a real logical tendril to reality. I apologise. I correct. My counsel -- I apologise that -- it was Varda I was thinking of. Hamdija Vilic. The Prosecution brought him, the Court invited him to come and talk about the possibility of being bribed. He says that the Milan Lukic Defence or persons related to him offered him 100.000 Euros to testify. What to testify to? That he was fighting some unknown Serbs on a certain day; not that he saw Milan Lukic, not that he kissed Milan Lukic, not that he was with Milan Lukic, but that a fight happened. Just a fight. We didn't need Hamdija Vilic to establish that. We have a dead commander documented by the repeater. They've argued in their submissions that, this road, look at it, it's a map, they show a map on the road. If you'd go there, Your Honour, this is a mountainous, heavily forested area that could be -- you could put three guys on a hill-side with guns, and no one's going to get past a stretch of road if they don't feel like it. This is the most convincing bit of evidence that Hamdija Vilic is just wacky, crazy, or lying, and the Court was distracted when this bit of evidence came in. It was distracted because you had just received some news on a filing, and this piece of evidence is important because if you look at number one, that was Vlade who sat next to me for so long in this courtroom. Vlade was with Mr. Vilic for supposedly an hour, yet he couldn't pick him out of a lineup that was prepared by the Prosecution. Vlade supposedly offered him 100.000 Euros, and he couldn't pick him out, but look at these green ones. Hamdija Vilic said that number 3 was Milan and number 8 was Sredoje. These are Dutch criminals, so that's how good Hamdija is on remembering things. Bikavac, 27th of June, 1992, allegedly. Again, the ID of Milan Lukic. Well, we know VG-114 or Zehra Turjacanin came in here and couldn't identify anybody. She looked around the room and said no. Of the other people that supposedly identified him, they were in a proximity to the alleged location that they should be dead right now. What no one's really accommodated for is why people in this neighbourhood would not be dead along with everyone else, and all you have to do is look at the aerial to show this. This is a high-up aerial, but it doesn't do us justice. Here we go. This is the one that's been the exhibit so many times with so many different people. In the corner of the road, if you look in the upper-hand corner, that's the location of the Meho Aljic house, upper left-hand corner, rather, and there's about 30 homes in that triangle, and yet all these supposed survivors/witnesses had to have been in that circle, and yet they're all here to talk about it. More importantly, they were all at the refugee camp with Ms. Turjacanin. They all took care of her. They all spoke with her. I believe they all came to love her. Zehra Turjacanin, the sole alleged survivor, 70 of her family neighbours and Muslim friends were put into this house, yet she only remembered 11 names, and of the 11 names only 3 of them had biographical information associated with them in Visegrad according to Ewa Tabeau, out of 70. And yet, out of 70, where did they come from? Were they bused in? If you had gone there, Your Honour, the streets are so narrow two Jugos can't pass each other without someone pulling into a driveway. That is a steep hill-side of which made the clutch smell just trying to get up the hill to Bikavac. So they didn't bus them in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did they walk them in like they stay in Pionirska? How? She claimed to escape through a tiny -- go ahead. This is important, Your Honour. She claims to have been burned in the home, yet she told soldiers and doctors that she was burned a different way. The nature of her burns are consistent with the history she reported to the doctors and the soldiers, which was: I caught myself on fire, my long flowing hair that was done down to my back. I caught it on a stove. I had a fit. She denies ever saying that, but guess what? It's in the transcript. It's in her earlier statement. It's in video. She told people she was burned in a household accident, and guess what, Your Honour? If you had long hair and it's on fire, what is going to happen when you put it out? Your hands are in the fire, and your sleeves pulled down as you raise it up. She only had burns from her eyebrows up and only her forehead. The scalp was protected. Why? By her hair. It was cut off in the video. You see the pictures, and it's on her ear-tips. That is her hair on fire, Your Honour. That's her hair, and had she -- but she says in her statement she burned her arms on a door that was so hot from the fire that it caused her to burn. Well, one, that kind of hot metal wouldn't cause burns on the back-side of your arm. You need to be enveloped in the fire for that. And if the door was that enveloped in the fire, to get that hot, how could she escape through it? Another thing is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. She was -- she supposedly was put in the house with 70 other people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: She gets in there. If the window -- if the windows are all covered in furniture and the door is covered by a garage door, then how are they throwing rocks through the windows? Then how do they shoot through the windows? Then grenades come in through the windows, then white powder that nobody has ever heard about or established as a viable accelerant comes in, and all of a sudden, poof, everyone's supposedly on fire? It makes no sense, but the most telling thing to me that Ms. Turjacanin is a hysterical witness is why police departments withhold -- see, I mean -- they are telling me to slow down a bunch, Your Honour, and that's why I had asked for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may have another five minutes. We'll stop at quarter past. That of course would be the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So Ms. Turjacanin then supposedly escapes. She escapes out, and what happened? Again, go ahead, next one. This is where Ms. Turjacanin denied telling others that she was in fact burned by the gas cylinder despite being shown her own testimony. This is important, Your Honour, because this is the original opening statement for the Prosecution, and this is where they identified the fire to be. This is what Ms. Turjacanin identified as the similar if not identical garage door as well as marking up that same photograph, but here is the important one. This is -- that opening's 9 inches wide. That's a tight fit for anybody, especially in loose clothing, but look at that picture to the right, Your Honour. One, the garage door is not high enough to block off your average patio door because it's too short. It's 5 foot, 4 inches tall. But if you look at the site just a few years back, not a picture used by the Prosecution, there's actually a shed garage with a blue car parked on the site of Bikavac, and yet it's the house in front that's burnt out, and as far as we know that site could have been vacant there for many, many years, no history given. Again, the door is too short, the window is too small. This is interesting. One, these are Zehra's identifications of where she passed. Why this is important? Because if you look on her diagram, she goes by the same orchard where -- where? VG-115 says she was hiding, where Zehra says that the police or soldiers were also hiding. Again, I draw the geometric shape at the top to illustrate. If not from this area, where did the victims come from that Zehra describes? And you have a young lady in shock with second and third degree burns trying to go through the June undergrowth of Bosnia? How could she do this, run around all these homes to warn them away in that state? You look at these competing diagrams as to where everyone put Bikavac. Well, the one big problem is is that these witnesses -- if VG-035 is over here at the top right-hand corner, if she's that close, why wasn't she rounded up and put there? If you look down to, oops, VG-58, VG-58 put the house on the wrong street completely. Cliff, that's his diagram at the bottom. VG-115 is hanging out with the assailants. That's because, if you look at this, to accelerate a little bit, the orchard that Ms. VG-115 says she was at is also where Zehra Turjacanin describes she gets out of the door, she's burning up, and there are these soldiers that don't shoot her because they must be out of bullets. Then they tell her, Stop, stop, and they don't come after her because maybe they are on drugs. Why? Because they all have Band-Aids on their arms, and then she wanders off and goes off on to the night. Do you realise how silly that sounds. One, I come from a neighbourhood where there's quite a few -- grew up where there was quite a few guys who would abuse heroin. I don't think any one of them used a Band-Aid when they would put that on their arm if they were just all going to party; one, the sequencing events makes no sense. If Ms. Turjacanin is on fire and she gets out, when did these guys have time to go start shooting up because if they were, like, going to hang outside and watch it go down, but they're going to start shooting up, then you put VG-115 in the picture, well, she's right on top of them and either hanging out with them or whatever. The fact of the matter is, though, is it makes no sense that a bunch of soldiers that are otherwise willing to put you and kill you wouldn't just club you or catch you or something in the state that Ms. Turjacanin claims to have gotten out and walked right by them. This is a big one. Zehra Turjacanin's brother and the statements by her brother directly dispute her rendition in two major points -- three major points, one of which is Milan Lukic was an associate of her brother's and: I met him through him. In his statement specifically, he states: I never -- or my sister never met Milan Lukic through me. Why would he do that unless it was a big deal? Secondly, Milan Lukic supposedly -- excuse me. Her brother supposedly was walled up in a home, and it was Zehra's warnings that got him broken out. In his statement, he states: I was out of there before the 27th. Therefore, he wasn't even there. And more importantly, Your Honour, is he makes no reference in his statements to have even heard his sister's story, because if he supposedly carried her to Medjedja for four days, I would think that Ms. Turjacanin would tell her brother what happened to her, and he would be willing to tell it to authorities and investigators, but he did not. More importantly, Your Honour, Ms. Turjacanin is fabricating because she was so adamant about Mitar Vasiljevic being there, so much so she wept when she was notified that Mitar was arrested. She identified him readily at a photo array, of course indicating that she knew who he was not but not necessarily that he killed anybody, and she never thought he'd have an alibi that he was in a hospital with a broken leg at the time. I believe Ms. Turjacanin is a true victim. I believe worse in certain ways may have happened to her than even the allegations as they stand. I think she should be evaluated and treated because she is a true victim. I believe she is simply fabricating the allegations. And as Mr. Jenkins stated, the fires may not have even happened. Again, this illustration goes to show that we have presented copious amounts of unrebutted alibi evidence. This is just to sort of poke fun, if you will, a little bit, but it's very serious, is that the OTP is changing their theory. They first stated he was the White Eagle commander. Now it's just the Lukic gang. I would argue simply that he was a soldier, and at two months into the war he had no real authority whatsoever as a reserve police officer and soldier. And this was the best evidence of the White Eagles. There's that skull and cross-bones that, lo and behold, we brought witnesses that identified these guys as Stevo and Josip, the camp cooks. And, again, this goes to illustrate that the Prosecution is evolving their case to suit, really, the evidence we brought, because we spent half this trial fighting to prove that Milan Lukic was a reserve police officer deserving of whatever role that put him in. We would argue, Your Honour, by this slide that the Prosecution picks and chooses when they want to believe our witness or their witness or when they don't because there have been certain times when they've stated that their witness is not reliable but only when it helps the Defence of Milan Lukic. This is just to illustrate that every single witness that said they saw Mitar Vasiljevic at Pionirska or Bikavac was lying, not mistaken but lying, because he was so well known and so well identified in photo arrays that there's no way to draw any other conclusion. The Prosecution brought up the Koran. The only people, there was no complaints from a single witness of the OTP or for fear. The only people that complained about the Koran in the courtroom was Nerma Jelacic [phoen] and Bakira Hasecic. That's it. That's where all the stink was about. Mr. Lukic got that Koran from a Muslim general. He brought it for his own reasons to make a point but not to bring fear to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to start closing now, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The last slide was of all the main leaders. A couple of them are standing trial or getting ready to stand for here. They've already stood trial. But they forgot. See, Bakira Hasecic named one of that I would -- defended one that I would argue is one of the main people to be accused in Visegrad: Brano Savovic. Why? Because she knew him. She knew him from before the war. She used to work with him. So we have no information that he, Savovic, has blood on his hands, but they were there the whole time and saw what was happening. Now, why that's important, Your Honours, is if you look at Visegrad as it stands, it's a very simple town to cut off. There's one road in from the forth, one road in from the south, there's -- all you need is three or four check-points. You mean to tell me Milan Lukic could run rampant around this town under the authorities' noses unless he wasn't either part of the establishment or under the direction of the establishment? These are all of the witnesses that are associated with the Association of Women Victims of War. These are all suspect because what is the motive? If you look at all the reports and all the news from this case, Your Honour, Milan Lukic was more accused of rape than anything. So what would be a reason to fabricate but attempting to get justice for an unindicted crime, an unindicted allegation? Why would people come and say one thing when they simply want you to go down and it has nothing to do with anything? The Court is very well aware of people that have felt threatened by this association and that have been told that they would lose their pensions or that they should testify wrongfully or untruthfully against Milan Lukic for rape. If that is the issue and if that is what is behind this case, all of the evidence of the OTP must be scrutinised accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid. You've gone beyond the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know if you wish to finish with a flourish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know how flourish that we could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- other than -- I think that the reality is is there was a real interest in this case that's separate from the crimes involved, and I believe that the Prosecution did not investigate the crimes in advance to the degree of which they brought a credible case before the Court. I think that the evidence falls well short of a conviction and that you should acquit Mr. Lukic on all counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that the last slide shown with all the witnesses who had statements with the Association of Women Victims of War be redacted. Those are all -- or many of them are victims of sexual crimes, and this would be a public reference to that fact, so could I ask that slide not -- be redacted from the public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be redacted. We'll adjourn and we resume tomorrow, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th of May, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.20 p.m.,
